title: LocalDate: Creating, Querying, and Comparing Dates
description: Create LocalDate instances using now(), of(), and parse(). Query fields with getYear(), getMonth(), getDayOfWeek(). Compare dates with isBefore(), isAfter(), and isEqual().
hints: LocalDate.of(year, month, day) — month is 1-based (1=January).
LocalDate.parse(string) expects ISO format yyyy-MM-dd by default.
getMonth() returns a Month enum; getMonthValue() returns the int (1-12).
getDayOfWeek() returns a DayOfWeek enum with a getDisplayName() method.

solution.explanation: LocalDate is an immutable, timezone-free date (year-month-day). It is the right type for birthdays, holidays, and business dates where time-of-day is irrelevant. LocalDate.now() queries the system clock using the default timezone for the date — if you need reproducible tests, pass a fixed Clock. LocalDate.of() is the factory for known dates; month argument is 1-based (unlike the old Calendar which was 0-based). parse() uses DateTimeFormatter.ISO_LOCAL_DATE by default, which expects yyyy-MM-dd. isLeapYear() follows the Gregorian rule: divisible by 4, but not by 100, unless also divisible by 400 — so 2000 and 2024 are leap years but 1900 is not.

title: LocalDate Arithmetic: plusDays, minusMonths, until (ChronoUnit)
description: Add and subtract days, weeks, and months from a LocalDate. Measure the difference between two dates in various units using ChronoUnit.between().
hints: LocalDate is immutable — all arithmetic methods return NEW LocalDate objects.
ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(start, end) returns a long — works for large ranges.
You can also use start.until(end, ChronoUnit.MONTHS) — same result, different syntax.

solution.explanation: LocalDate arithmetic methods always return new instances — LocalDate is immutable just like String. start.plusDays(90) does not modify start; you must capture the result. When adding months, Java handles month-length overflow: if you add 1 month to January 31, you get February 28/29 (the last valid day of February), not March 2 or 3. ChronoUnit.between() truncates to whole units: 365 days / 7 = 52.14... → 52 whole weeks. The months computation counts only complete calendar months — Dec 31 minus Jan 1 is 11 months and 30 days, so months=11. until(end, unit) is the instance-method variant of ChronoUnit.unit.between(this, end).

title: LocalDateTime: Creation, Component Access, and truncation
description: Work with LocalDateTime — a date combined with a time. Create instances, extract components, and truncate to different time units.
hints: LocalDateTime.of(date, time) combines a LocalDate and a LocalTime.
atTime(time) on a LocalDate returns a LocalDateTime; atDate(date) on a LocalTime does the same.
truncatedTo(ChronoUnit.HOURS) zeroes out minutes, seconds, and nanoseconds.

solution.explanation: LocalDateTime bundles a date and a time without any timezone information — it is useful for scheduling events where the context (timezone) is known implicitly, such as a local calendar. LocalDateTime.of(int year, int month, int day, int hour, int minute, int second) has a convenient flat overload. LocalDate.atTime(time) is the fluent way to compose a LocalDateTime from its parts. truncatedTo(ChronoUnit) zeroes all fields smaller than the specified unit: truncatedTo(HOURS) sets minutes=0, seconds=0, nanos=0. Note that LocalDateTime lacks timezone context, so it cannot represent a unique point in time across different time zones — use ZonedDateTime or Instant for that.

title: ZonedDateTime: Working Across Time Zones
description: Create ZonedDateTime objects, convert between timezones, and understand the difference between withZoneSameInstant (converts the moment) and withZoneSameLocal (reinterprets the clock).
hints: ZoneId.of("America/New_York") uses IANA timezone IDs — never use 3-letter abbreviations like 'EST'.
withZoneSameInstant: converts the moment — the physical time doesn't change, just the display zone.
withZoneSameLocal: keeps the clock reading but changes the zone — shifts the underlying instant.
ZoneId.getAvailableZoneIds() returns a Set<String> of all available zone IDs.

solution.explanation: ZonedDateTime = LocalDateTime + ZoneId + the current offset (which may change for DST). Always use full IANA zone IDs like 'America/New_York' — abbreviations like 'EST' are ambiguous (used by multiple zones) and not reliably parsed. withZoneSameInstant is the 'convert' operation: it takes the same absolute moment and changes how it is displayed — London 09:00 BST (UTC+1) is simultaneously New York 04:00 EDT (UTC-4), 13 hours apart. withZoneSameLocal is the 'reinterpret' operation: it keeps the clock reading (09:00) but stamps it with the new zone — this changes the underlying UTC instant. Use withZoneSameInstant for 'what time is it there right now?' and withZoneSameLocal almost never (it is a data transformation that should usually be avoided).

title: Duration and Period: Measuring Time Gaps
description: Use Duration (time-based: hours, minutes, seconds) and Period (date-based: years, months, days) to measure and represent gaps between temporal objects.
hints: Duration.between() works on time-based temporals (LocalTime, LocalDateTime, Instant).
Period.between() works on date-based temporals (LocalDate, LocalDate).
Duration.toMinutes() returns TOTAL minutes, not just the minutes component.
Period.getYears() returns just the year component, not total years — use ChronoUnit.YEARS.between() for total.

solution.explanation: Duration models an exact time span in nanoseconds — appropriate for time-of-day or instant differences. Period models a date-based span in years-months-days — appropriate for calendar differences where month lengths vary. The crucial gotcha: Duration.toMinutes() returns the TOTAL duration in minutes (e.g. 8h30m = 510 total minutes), NOT just the minutes component. Java 9 introduced toMinutesPart(), toSecondsPart() etc. which return only the component (30 for minutes in this case). Period.getYears() returns only the year part of the period, not the total number of years — use ChronoUnit.YEARS.between() if you need the total. Never mix Duration and Period — Duration cannot be added to a LocalDate (has no concept of 'a day') and Period cannot be added to a LocalTime.

title: DateTimeFormatter: format() and parse()
description: Format LocalDate and LocalDateTime to human-readable strings using pattern-based and built-in formatters. Parse strings back to date objects.
hints: DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("MMMM d, yyyy") creates a custom formatter; MMMM = full month name.
DateTimeFormatter is immutable and thread-safe — safe to store as a static final field.
DateTimeFormatter.ofLocalizedDate(FormatStyle.FULL).withLocale(Locale.FRENCH) for locale-aware.
For parsing, use LocalDate.parse(string, formatter) or formatter.parse(string, LocalDate::from).

solution.explanation: DateTimeFormatter uses a pattern language similar to SimpleDateFormat but is immutable and thread-safe — SimpleDateFormat was notoriously NOT thread-safe. Pattern letters: M/MM/MMM/MMMM = 7/07/Jul/July; d/dd = 4/04; yyyy = 2024; HH:mm = 24-hour time. Format.FULL, LONG, MEDIUM, SHORT are locale-sensitive styles that delegate to the locale's date formatting rules — great for internationalised apps. Always specify a Locale with named patterns to avoid JVM default locale surprises: 'MMM' in German would produce 'Mär' instead of 'Mar'. ISO formatters are built-in constants and parse/format ISO-8601 strings without any pattern string — prefer them for data interchange (APIs, databases).

title: Custom DateTimeFormatter with ofLocalizedDateTime and withResolverStyle
description: Build formatters with optional sections, handle lenient vs strict parsing with ResolverStyle, and format zone-aware date-times.
hints: EEE = short day name (Mon, Tue...), EEEE = full day name.
z = timezone abbreviation (EDT), Z = numeric offset (+0000), VV = IANA zone ID.
DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern(pattern).withResolverStyle(ResolverStyle.STRICT).
STRICT mode rejects Feb-30; LENIENT mode rolls it over to Mar-01 or Mar-02.

solution.explanation: ResolverStyle controls how the parsed field values are assembled into a date. STRICT: every field must be in range for the given month/year — Feb-30 is rejected. SMART (default): out-of-range day-of-month is clipped to the last valid day — Feb-30 becomes Feb-29 in a leap year or Feb-28 otherwise. LENIENT: overflows roll over — Feb-30 in 2024 becomes March 1 (Feb has 29 days in 2024, so +1 day overflows to March 1). Use STRICT for data validation (rejecting bad input), LENIENT when performing date calculations where overflow is intentional. Note: with STRICT you should use 'u' (proleptic year) instead of 'y' (year-of-era) to avoid ambiguity with BC years.

title: Instant: Machine Time and Epoch Milliseconds
description: Use Instant to represent a precise point on the UTC timeline. Convert between Instant and epoch milliseconds, and understand when to use Instant vs LocalDateTime.
hints: Instant.now() always uses UTC — it has no timezone.
instant.toEpochMilli() returns milliseconds since 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z.
Instant.ofEpochMilli(ms) creates an Instant from epoch milliseconds.
To display an Instant in a human-readable way, convert: instant.atZone(zoneId).

solution.explanation: Instant represents a single point on the UTC timeline — the number of nanoseconds since the Unix epoch (1970-01-01T00:00:00Z). It has no timezone and cannot be formatted to show day/month/year without first converting to a ZonedDateTime. Instant is ideal for: logging timestamps, storing 'when did this happen' in databases (as a UTC value), measuring elapsed time, and comparing event order. LocalDateTime is NOT suitable for these because it lacks timezone context — the 'same' LocalDateTime means different instants in different timezones. Rule of thumb: if you're thinking about users and calendars, use LocalDate/LocalDateTime; if you're thinking about the machine, logging, or data storage, use Instant.

title: Bridging Legacy java.util.Date and java.util.Calendar
description: Convert between the legacy java.util.Date/Calendar API and the modern java.time API. Essential when working with older libraries like JDBC, JPA, or Jackson that haven't fully migrated.
hints: Date.toInstant() is the bridge into modern API. java.util.Date.from(instant) goes the other way.
To get a LocalDate from an Instant: instant.atZone(ZoneId.systemDefault()).toLocalDate()
Calendar.toInstant() works the same as Date.toInstant().
LocalDateTime has no timezone — you must provide one when converting to Date: ldt.atZone(zone).toInstant()

solution.explanation: java.util.Date is essentially a thin wrapper around a long (epoch milliseconds), and toInstant() exposes that directly. The conversion chain Date -> Instant -> ZonedDateTime -> LocalDate is the standard idiom. You MUST go through ZonedDateTime when extracting a LocalDate from an Instant because the calendar date depends on the timezone — the same Instant can be 'June 15' in New York but 'June 16' in Tokyo. ZoneId.systemDefault() uses the JVM's configured timezone — fine for user-facing apps, but for servers always prefer an explicit zone. Calendar.toInstant() was added in Java 8 as a convenience — previously you had to call cal.getTimeInMillis() and use ofEpochMilli(). For JDBC, use PreparedStatement.setTimestamp() with a Timestamp.from(instant) bridge.

title: TemporalAdjusters: First/Last Day of Month, Next Weekday
description: Use TemporalAdjusters to navigate to meaningful calendar positions like the first Monday of the month, last day of the month, or the next occurrence of a specific weekday.
hints: TemporalAdjusters.firstDayOfMonth() / lastDayOfMonth() return the start/end of the month.
TemporalAdjusters.firstInMonth(DayOfWeek) returns the first occurrence of that day.
TemporalAdjusters.next(DayOfWeek) skips to the NEXT occurrence (never returns today).
TemporalAdjusters.nextOrSame(DayOfWeek) returns today if today matches, otherwise the next.

solution.explanation: TemporalAdjusters is a utility class of factory methods that create TemporalAdjuster instances — functional interfaces that take a Temporal and return a new Temporal. LocalDate.with(adjuster) applies the adjuster and returns a new LocalDate. firstInMonth(DOW) finds the first occurrence of that day in the current month — March 2024 starts on a Friday so the first Monday is March 4. next(DOW) always moves forward at least one day, while nextOrSame(DOW) stays if the day already matches. lastInMonth(DOW) works backward from the end of the month. You can write custom adjusters with TemporalAdjusters.ofDateAdjuster(UnaryOperator<LocalDate>) — the example computes the next business day, correctly skipping the weekend after Friday.

title: DST Transitions: Handling Clock Changes Correctly
description: Understand how Daylight Saving Time (DST) gaps and overlaps affect ZonedDateTime calculations, and why Duration.ofHours(1) across a DST transition doesn't always add 1 calendar hour.
hints: Adding Duration.ofHours(1) to a ZonedDateTime adds exactly 3600 seconds to the instant.
At a spring-forward gap, the result is automatically pushed forward past the missing hour.
withEarlierOffsetAtOverlap() and withLaterOffsetAtOverlap() disambiguate overlap times.

solution.explanation: DST creates two anomalies: gaps (spring forward, when a local time simply doesn't exist) and overlaps (fall back, when a local time occurs twice). Adding Duration to a ZonedDateTime always adds exact seconds to the underlying instant — it never 'skips' time. At the spring-forward gap, the instant lands in a non-existent local time window; ZonedDateTime automatically adjusts by applying the new offset, so the clock jumps from 01:30 to 03:30. At fall-back overlaps, ZonedDateTime defaults to the earlier (pre-clock-change) offset. withEarlierOffsetAtOverlap() explicitly picks the first occurrence (EDT, UTC-4) and withLaterOffsetAtOverlap() picks the second (EST, UTC-5). These two ZonedDateTimes represent instants that are exactly 1 hour apart. This matters for scheduling (recurring jobs, reminders) and for audit logs that need to distinguish which '01:30' was meant.

title: Building a Meeting Scheduler with LocalDateTime
description: Apply LocalDateTime arithmetic to schedule recurring weekly meetings, check for conflicts, and compute time until the next occurrence.
hints: Generate with a loop: nextMeeting = firstMeeting.plusWeeks(i) for i in 0..n-1.
Two meetings a and b overlap if a.start < b.end AND b.start < a.end.
timeUntilNext: filter meetings where meeting.isAfter(now), find the min, return Duration.between(now, min).

solution.explanation: plusWeeks(i) is equivalent to plusDays(7*i) but reads more clearly. The overlap test uses the standard interval intersection formula: [a, aEnd) overlaps [b, bEnd) if and only if a < bEnd AND b < aEnd. Note that touching (a == bEnd) is NOT an overlap (meetings back-to-back are fine). The Stream pipeline in timeUntilNext() filters to future meetings, finds the minimum (closest in time), and maps to a Duration — the Optional handles the case where all meetings are in the past. Duration.between(now, next) gives the exact time gap. The output 'PT15M' is ISO-8601 duration notation: P=period, T=time section, 15M=15 minutes. Use duration.toMinutes() to convert to a readable number if needed.
